passage: I'm Neelam, and I sit next to Chaitanya in Statistics. There was a stretch last term when Chaitanya skipped classes and would only say that the "group" had been a mistake. In March Chaitanya joined the badminton club, first turning up late and leaving early, then staying on for the tea. A study circle started on Thursdays in the library and Chaitanya brought notes to it. Twice I saw Chaitanya walk into the counselling office with head down and come out looking tired but a bit lighter. Yesterday, in the canteen, Chaitanya laughed at a joke, properly. I can't know what happened in that group or what was said to the counsellor. I only notice that there are more people around Chaitanya now, and I'm glad about it.

qa.a: Chaitanya joined the badminton club and a Thursday study circle in the library.

passage:
January. Two weeks after Harish stopped going to the "brotherhood" meetings, the evenings were the worst. No one called. The group had filled every night for a year, and now his room felt enormous. Part of him missed them, and he hated that.
February. On the college counsellor's advice, he did two things. He joined the Tuesday and Friday football sessions at the sports club near the hostel, and a study circle for his statistics paper. He also kept seeing Vasudha, the counsellor, every other week. "I feel stupid," he told her once. "Like I should have seen it." She asked what he'd been looking for when he joined. "People," he said. "Just people."
April. After a Friday match, four players dragged him to a dhaba. He laughed so hard at their stories that he forgot to check his phone. That night he realised he hadn't thought about the group for three days.

qa.q: Which days did Harish play football?
qa.a: He played on Tuesdays and Fridays.

qa.q: How was Harish feeling in January, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt lonely and ashamed of missing the group, with his room feeling enormous and no one calling.

qa.q: What else could Harish do to keep his new circle strong?
qa.a: He could invite a teammate or study-circle friend to meet outside the sessions, so the new connections deepen.

qa.q: How might Vasudha see Harish's answer that he was looking for 'people'?
qa.a: Vasudha likely sees it as a key insight, showing that the need for connection, not stupidity, drew him in.

grounding: Shows the person, after leaving a group, joining a sports club and study circle and seeing a counsellor about shame to meet the need for belonging.

subtype: Approach: rebuild belonging through healthy communities [Revision]
passage:
"Salma, you asked how I stopped feeling empty after I left that group. I'm Shalini, and I'll tell you honestly, it didn't stop in a day.
I was twenty-two. For two years that group was my whole life: dinners, songs, trips. When I left, I lost all of it at once. And I felt such shame. How could a smart girl fall for that?
My mistake at first was staying home, alone, so no one could see. I was so lonely I nearly went back.
Then my college counsellor said something simple: 'You didn't join for their ideas. You joined because you needed people. So find people.' I joined the badminton club at the community centre and a Sunday reading circle at the library. And I kept talking to her about the shame.
Six months later I had friends who didn't need anything from me except to show up. That's what made going back impossible."

qa.q: What did Shalini join after the counsellor's advice?
qa.a: The badminton club at the community centre and a Sunday reading circle at the library.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel right after leaving the group?
qa.a: Shalini felt empty, lonely and ashamed, hiding at home and nearly going back.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Shalini's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: The counsellor's words about needing people were the turning point, because they made her look for healthy groups instead of hiding.

qa.q: How might the counsellor have felt seeing Shalini six months later?
qa.a: The counsellor would likely feel glad and reassured to see Shalini with friends who needed nothing but her company.

grounding: Shows a person after leaving a group joining a sports club and reading circle and talking to a counsellor about shame, filling the need for belonging.
